name: RW Aurigae
kind: A young star that dims unpredictably behind clouds of dust

evidence.classification: Known variable star, quiet in these snapshots
evidence.confidence_note: lowered because most SPHEREx measurements are saturated

checks.text: Steady brightness between Sep 2025 and Mar 2026 (+0.03 ± 0.06 mag)
140 of 150 SPHEREx measurements flagged (overflow or bloom: the object is too bright for SPHEREx). The spectrum uses the 10 clean ones.
Catalogued as a variable star, but these SPHEREx visits show no change larger than the measurement uncertainty. A few snapshots can miss a change that happens between them.

numbers.label: apparent drift (below the detection limit, not a real motion)

changes.method: Dots seen only in WISE 2010 are paired with dots seen only in SPHEREx at 4.6 µm, 8″ to 190″ apart and of similar brightness. Each pair is then checked against the target's path, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.
changes.not_checked: Asteroids and comets are not checked. An unconfirmed pair is not a discovery.

facts.headline: About 510 light-years away
facts.detail: The light in these images left it about 510 years ago.

limits: Motion: an object must shift 2 SPHEREx pixels (12″) to count as moving. Over these 15.7 years that means faster than 0.78″ per year. Slower objects read as “no measurable motion”.
SPHEREx alone covers only 6 months here: by the same 2-pixel rule, enough only for motion faster than 26″ per year. The 2010 WISE image is what makes slower motion visible.
Brightness: compared at 2 SPHEREx visits only. A change between or outside those dates is not seen.
Bright stars: this one overflows SPHEREx pixels, so its spectrum and exact brightness are not reliable here.
Solar System: the page checks against Gaia stars only. It does not check asteroids or comets, so a moving dot without a Gaia circle may be a known asteroid.
Crowding: one SPHEREx pixel is 6.15″ wide, so two close objects can blend into one dot and one spectrum.
